title: Resonance in Oscillatory Systems
short_intro: Resonance is a physical phenomenon in which a vibrating system or external force drives another system to oscillate with greater amplitude at specific frequencies. It occurs when the frequency of an externally applied periodic force matches the natural frequency of the driven system.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of resonance, condition for resonance, mechanical and acoustic resonance, examples such as tuning forks, simple pendulum, and basic resonance tube experiments.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Mathematical treatment of forced oscillations, amplitude and phase resonance, sharpness of resonance, quality factor (Q-factor), electrical LCR resonance circuits, and power absorption.

prerequisites: Damped harmonic oscillations and damping coefficient

concept_notes.heading: Condition for Resonance
bullets: Resonance occurs in a forced oscillator when the angular frequency of the driving force (omega) equals the natural frequency (omega_0) of the system.
At resonance, the velocity of the oscillating system is exactly in phase with the driving force, resulting in maximum power transfer.
The amplitude of oscillation reaches its maximum value, limited solely by the damping present in the system.

concept_notes.heading: Amplitude and Phase at Resonance
bullets: The steady-state amplitude of a forced damped oscillator is inversely proportional to the damping coefficient when omega = omega_0.
The phase difference between the displacement and the driving force is exactly pi/2 radians (90 degrees) at resonance.
The maximum amplitude does not occur precisely at omega = omega_0 when damping is present, but at a slightly lower frequency given by omega = sqrt(omega_0^2 - 2beta^2).

concept_notes.heading: Sharpness of Resonance and Q-Factor
bullets: The sharpness of the resonance curve describes how rapidly the amplitude drops as the driving frequency deviates from the natural frequency.
The Quality factor (Q-factor) is a dimensionless parameter that measures the sharpness of resonance and energy storage relative to energy dissipation.
A system with light damping exhibits a high Q-factor, a very sharp resonance peak, and sustained oscillations.

concept_notes.heading: Acoustic and Electrical Resonance
bullets: Acoustic resonance occurs in air columns, such as in Kundt's tube or resonance column apparatus, producing stationary longitudinal waves with displacement nodes and anti-nodes.
Electrical resonance occurs in series or parallel LCR circuits when the inductive reactance equals the capacitive reactance (X_L = X_C).
At electrical resonance, the impedance of a series LCR circuit is purely resistive and reaches its minimum value, maximizing the circuit current.

derivations.title: Amplitude and Phase of Forced Damped Oscillations
derivations.conditions: A particle of mass m subjected to restoring force -kx, damping force -bv, and driving force F_0 cos(omega t).
steps: Write the equation of motion: m(d^2x/dt^2) + b(dx/dt) + kx = F_0 cos(omega t).
Substitute trial solution x = A cos(omega t - phi) and solve for steady-state amplitude A = (F_0/m) / sqrt((omega_0^2 - omega^2)^2 + (4 beta^2 omega^2)), where omega_0^2 = k/m and beta = b/(2m).
Determine the phase lag phi between displacement and driving force from tan(phi) = (2 beta omega) / (omega_0^2 - omega^2).
derivations.result: A = (F_0/m) / sqrt((omega_0^2 - omega^2)^2 + 4 beta^2 omega^2) and tan(phi) = 2 beta omega / (omega_0^2 - omega^2)

derivations.title: Resonant Frequency and Quality Factor of Series LCR Circuit
derivations.conditions: Alternating voltage source connected to a resistor R, inductor L, and capacitor C in series.
steps: Write the total impedance Z of the circuit: Z = R + j(omega L - 1/(omega C)).
Apply the resonance condition where the imaginary part of impedance is zero: omega_r L = 1/(omega_r C).
Solve for resonant angular frequency omega_r = 1/sqrt(LC) and define the quality factor Q = omega_r L / R.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Amplitude-Frequency Resonance Curves
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A family of curves plotting steady-state amplitude (A) versus driving frequency (omega) for different values of damping coefficient (b).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that as damping decreases, the resonance peak becomes higher and narrower. The maximum amplitude shifts slightly to the left of omega_0 for larger damping.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in conceptual questions regarding the effect of damping on resonance height and sharpness.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Resonance Column Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A vertical glass tube filled with water, connected to a reservoir, with a vibrating tuning fork held above the open mouth.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Determines the velocity of sound in air by locating successive resonant lengths (l_1 and l_2) corresponding to stationary wave anti-nodes at the open end.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Core practical experiment for TGT and PGT examinations, testing end correction and wavelength calculation.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Series LCR Resonance Curve (Current vs Frequency)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A bell-shaped curve showing current (I) on the y-axis against frequency (f) on the x-axis, featuring half-power points at I_max / sqrt(2).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates frequency selectivity in electrical circuits. The distance between half-power frequencies defines the bandwidth.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in numericals involving bandwidth, resonant frequency, and quality factor calculation.

solved_numericals.question: A resonance air column tube shows resonance with a tuning fork of frequency 512 Hz at length 16.5 cm and 52.5 cm. Calculate the velocity of sound in air.
solution_steps: Recall the relation between wavelength and successive resonant lengths: lambda = 2(l_2 - l_1).
Substitute the given lengths: lambda = 2(0.525 m - 0.165 m) = 2(0.360 m) = 0.720 m.
Calculate the velocity of sound using v = f * lambda: v = 512 Hz * 0.720 m = 368.64 m/s.

solved_numericals.question: A series LCR circuit has an inductance L = 2 H, capacitance C = 32 microF, and resistance R = 10 ohms. Find the resonant frequency and the quality factor Q of the circuit.
solution_steps: Calculate resonant angular frequency omega_r = 1 / sqrt(LC) = 1 / sqrt(2 * 32 * 10^-6) = 1 / sqrt(64 * 10^-6) = 1 / (8 * 10^-3) = 125 rad/s.
Convert to linear frequency f_r = omega_r / (2 * pi) = 125 / (2 * 3.1416) = 19.89 Hz.
Calculate Q-factor using Q = omega_r L / R = (125 * 2) / 10 = 250 / 10 = 25.

solved_numericals.question: A forced oscillator has a mass of 1 kg, natural frequency 200 rad/s, and damping constant b = 2 kg/s. If a periodic driving force of peak value 10 N acts on it at resonance, calculate the maximum steady-state amplitude.
solution_steps: At resonance (omega = omega_0), the amplitude formula simplifies to A_max = F_0 / (2 beta omega_0) or F_0 / (b omega_0).
Identify values: F_0 = 10 N, b = 2 kg/s, omega_0 = 200 rad/s.
Substitute values into the formula: A_max = 10 / (2 * 200) = 10 / 400 = 0.025 m.

assumptions_and_limitations: Linearity assumption: Restoring forces are strictly proportional to displacement (Hooke's law holds), which fails at large amplitudes where anharmonic terms become significant.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Maximum amplitude always occurs exactly at the natural frequency omega_0.
common_misconceptions.correct: Maximum amplitude occurs at omega = sqrt(omega_0^2 - 2beta^2), which is slightly lower than omega_0 in damped systems.
common_misconceptions.why: Damping introduces a velocity-dependent term that shifts the peak frequency of the response curve.

common_misconceptions.wrong: At resonance, the phase difference between displacement and driving force is zero.
common_misconceptions.correct: At resonance, the phase difference between displacement and driving force is exactly pi/2 (90 degrees).
common_misconceptions.why: The velocity is in phase with the driving force at resonance, meaning displacement lags velocity by pi/2 and thus lags the driving force by pi/2.

quick_revision: Resonance occurs when the driving frequency matches the natural frequency, maximizing amplitude and energy transfer.
Amplitude of Forced Oscillation: A = \frac{F_0 / m}{\sqrt{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 + 4\beta^2\omega^2}}
